newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher, weak data feeling grows.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher, weak data feeling grows.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed higher for the second day in a row after a growing sentiment that key September payroll data may be on the weak side triggered some buying throughout the yield curve, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended up 14/32 at 98-27/32. Its yield was at 6.84 percent.

"It's not a lot of heavy buying. It's not a high demand sort of rally. But I think people are becoming more comfortable with the idea of a weak payroll number," said Patrick Dimick, economist at CS First Boston.

The September employment report will be issued on Friday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. In a Reuters survey, U.S. economists said they expect non-farm payrolls to grow by 166,000 in September, well below the 250,000 seen in August.
Average hourly earnings are forecast to be up 0.2 percent against the previous 0.5 percent rise.
If the expectations are confirmed, analysts said the data will support the idea of a slowing economy in the third quarter and of steady interest rates in the near future.
"Near-term we're looking for some softer data," said Lee Youngdahl, economist at Aubrey G. Lanston Co and Inc.
"I think the overall number will be held down by the reversal on the government sector employment ... which was very strong over the last two months," Youngdahl added.

Analysts said the sentiment sparked a mild buying spree which started in overnight trading. Foreign investors, including a large Japanese security firm and a bank portfolio, were said to be very active in the market.
The rise in Treasury prices have led scores of investors to either cover their previously-set short positions or take a more neutral approach to the market, pundits said.
"You don't want to be caught short ahead of the employment report the way things are shaping up," said a trader at a foreign investment bank here.
The short-covering bout started on Monday and spilled over into Tuesday's session, both domestic and overseas.
Some said, however, the market has now become more vulnerable to any possible surprises in the payroll report.

"We always have this volatility associated with employment ... There is some building up in the market this report should be okay. But still it also makes us more vulnerable to surprises," Dimick said.
Analysts said the market's technical outlook also contributed to the rise in prices. "The technical environment has been positive too," Youngdahl said.
The market shrugged off a 0.9 percent rise in the August construction data released on Wednesday against a revised 1.1 percent drop seen in the previous month, analysts said.
"The data were mostly a non-event today," a trader said.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed off seven basis points at 4.90 percent. The six-month bill rate was down five points at 5.09 percent.
The year bill rate was off five points at 5.29 percent.
The two-year note closed up 3/32 at 100-1/32. Its yield dropped below the psychological 6.0 percent barrier to end at 5.98 percent.
The five-year note traded up 7/32 at 100-5/32 to yield 6.34 percent. The ten-year note closed up 10/32 at 102-27/32, yielding 6.60 percent.
